newsitem.title: USA: Markets await key economic reports.
newsitem.headline: Markets await key economic reports.

text.p: The Wall Street bull is expected to continue its post-election stampede this week, although traders will be watching two pieces of data due in particular that could sent the market stumbling.

"(The bull market) is not over," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd. "Everybody is trying to get that little correction. But we are in the throw-in-towel mode for bears."
"A lot of numbers are going to be important" this week, said Hugh Johnson at First Albany Corp.
At the top of the list are Monday's report from the private National Association of Purchasing Management and Friday's Labour Department data on the November job market.
Economists estimate that payrolls grew 179,000 in November, compared with 210,000 in October. The November unemployment rate was seen unchanged at 5.2 percent.

Analysts expect that the purchasing manager's index rose to 50.8 in December, up slightly from November. A reading above 50 percent points to growth in the manufacturing sector, while one below that level indicates contraction.

Analysts will be watching two components of the purchasing manager's report especially closely: vendor deliveries and prices. The data are key indicators of the temperature of the economy and inflation and are watched carefully by the Federal Reserve, the nation's central bank, analysts said.

"If (the numbers) comes in as expected, the bond market is likely to continue to move up, and stock prices are also likely to move up," Johnson said. Falling long-term interest rates in the bond market have helped fuel the recent runup in stocks.
More and more analysts are saying the bull market will continue unimpeded in the near term.
"We're in the midst of a parabolic move," Bleier said. "There's no question we're in the midst of an extremely emotional move in the market."
Since Election Day, the Dow Jones industrial average has gained 440.52 points, or 7.2 percent.

"Everybody knows how expensive we are, yet it doesn't matter," Bleier said. "Money flow keeps coming fast and furious from funds. The question for the week ahead is how high can this parabolic move take us."

Some strategists noted that several blue-chip issues have scored strong gains, such as General Electric Co., Citicorp, Intel Corp. and Microsoft Corp. But others worried that the rising market was due to a lack of supply in fairly valued stocks.
Michael Metz at Oppenheimer & Co., said the market was facing a "supply vacuum" as portfolio managers were reluctant to give up blue-chip stocks that have performed well.
If money managers sold, they would have to hold cash or buy other issues that have not done as well.
"There's no reason for anyone to sell," he said. "What would you buy as a substitute?"
Metz predicted a rise in the next few weeks of secondary stocks and in "rumor stocks" -- those affected by talk of takeovers and restructurings.

He mentioned Quaker Oats Co., which is reportedly in talks to sell its Snapple line of drinks, and SmithKline Beecham Plc, which has been named as a possible takeover target of Roche, the big Swiss drug company.

Other reports due this week include construction spending for October, on Monday, leading indicators for October, on Tuesday, revised third quarter productivity and costs, on Thursday, and October factory orders, due on Friday.
